speaker: John Carmack
title: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets (#309)
question: In large production codebases, why do automated static analysis tools catch serious bugs that even elite engineering teams miss?
guest: The id Software code bases were a couple million lines of code, and we had a reputation for having some of the most robust code—Microsoft told us our Xbox crash count was so tiny it was probably literally hardware errors. Yet when I scrubbed the codebase with every static analysis tool I could find, it was shocking how many errors were in there: copy-paste bugs, printf format strings with the wrong data type that could cause crashes, missing null checks that could actually happen. Even in my own code, there were mines sitting there for a year waiting for us to step on. I reached the conclusion that anything syntactically allowed in your language is going to show up eventually in a large enough codebase. Good intentions aren't going to keep it from happening; you need automated tools and guardrails like static types and analyzers. Whatever stream of code you output, there is a statistical regularity of mistakes. I am more in favor of static analysis where you can't even run your program until you fix the flaw, rather than running it and hoping a unit test catches it.

points.core: Every programmer introduces defects at a steady statistical rate regardless of engineering skill.
points.note: Accept: even top developers inevitably emit recurring mistakes across large volumes of code; good intentions or discipline cannot eliminate human error rates. Do not credit: generic claims that humans are imperfect or need code reviews.

points.core: Any bug a programming language allows syntactically will eventually appear in large codebases.
points.note: Accept: at sufficient scale, every possible unsafe construct permitted by the language (e.g., null dereferences, format mismatches, copy-paste errors) inevitably manifests as latent landmines. Do not credit: listing random bug types without connecting scale to what the language permits.

points.core: Static analysis blocks flawed code before execution instead of relying on test coverage.
points.note: Accept: compile-time checks, static types, or analyzers prevent running broken paths upfront, unlike unit tests which only catch bugs on exercised paths. Do not credit: generic praise for automated testing or CI pipelines.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Static analysis tools win mainly because of scale and exhaustiveness, not because they are smarter than the engineers. Humans review code locally: a diff, a function, a file. Serious bugs, though, often live in interactions that span many files, modules, and teams, such as a null value returned in one place and dereferenced five calls away, a lock acquired in inconsistent orders, or tainted input reaching a sensitive sink. No reviewer can hold millions of lines and all their interprocedural paths in their head, but an analyzer can systematically explore them.

Tools also examine the paths humans neglect. Error handling, rare branches, and unusual configurations are seldom exercised by tests and are skimmed in review, yet that is where memory leaks, use-after-frees, and unchecked failures hide. Analyzers treat every path with equal attention and never get tired, rushed, or biased by assumptions like "this can't be null here."

Finally, they are consistent: once a bug pattern is encoded, it is checked everywhere, on every commit, including in old code nobody reads anymore. Engineers at Coverity, Google, and Meta have reported exactly this: the tools find real bugs in mature, well-tested code.

The response links codebase size to the difficulty of tracing cross-module bugs but never claims that scale makes language-permitted mistakes inevitable.
The response explains that analyzers can inspect paths tests rarely exercise but never says that a failed static check blocks execution.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Even elite engineers are bound by working-memory limits and review code primarily as localized diffs, relying on mental models of how the surrounding system behaves. In massive production codebases, however, serious bugs rarely stay confined to a single function; they emerge from non-local interactions across deep call graphs, asynchronous boundaries, and modules written years apart by different teams. When a change subtly alters an implicit contract—around nullability, lock ordering, object lifetime, or error propagation—human reviewers easily miss the broken assumption several layers away.

Static analysis tools excel precisely where human cognition falters. Rather than reasoning about intended behavior along common execution paths, they mechanically evaluate exact language semantics across vast combinations of branches simultaneously. Using techniques like interprocedural dataflow, taint tracking, and abstract interpretation, analyzers exhaustively trace untrusted inputs, rare failure modes, integer overflows, concurrency races, and resource leaks without fatigue or confirmation bias. Because they continuously verify invariants across the entire dependency graph rather than just the lines changed in a pull request, they catch silent cross-boundary mismatches that no human team could practically trace by hand.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Static analysis tools catch bugs that strong teams miss because of scale and attention, not because they're smarter. A large codebase has millions of execution paths. Engineers reason about the common "happy path," and reviewers usually look at a small diff without the whole system in their heads. An analyzer checks every path the same way each time. That includes rarely run error handlers, unusual branches, and interactions between functions spread across distant files and modules.

Many serious bugs are simple mistakes in places nobody looks: a null dereference after a failed allocation, a resource never released on an early return, an unchecked error code, an integer overflow, a data race between two modules owned by different teams. Yuan et al. (OSDI 2014) found that most catastrophic failures in distributed systems came from simple errors in error-handling code, which tests and reviewers rarely exercise. Tools also apply rules no human can enforce by hand across millions of lines and constant change, and they don't get tired, rushed or overconfident.

That's why Facebook's Infer and Google's Tricorder run inside code review, where findings arrive while the code is still fresh in the author's mind.

The response links scale to overlooked paths and lists defects without claiming that defects permitted by the language inevitably appear at sufficient scale.
The response describes findings delivered during code review without claiming that static checks block flawed code before execution.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Even elite engineers review code in localized diffs with finite working memory, whereas large production codebases span millions of lines and deep call chains. Static analysis tools excel where human cognition hits its limits: they build whole-program control-flow and data-flow graphs to trace nullability, taint, resource lifetimes, and lock ordering across dozens of files and indirect calls that no reviewer can track mentally.

They are also immune to fatigue, time pressure, and confirmation bias. Humans naturally skim familiar patterns and focus on the happy path, easily missing rare error branches, subtle integer overflows, or leaks during partial failures. Analyzers mechanically inspect every reachable path on every commit without tiring or assuming intent. Finally, as systems evolve, a harmless local edit can quietly violate an implicit contract in a distant module. Automated analysis continuously re-verifies those global invariants across the entire codebase, catching regressions that neither human reviewers nor standard test suites uncover.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Static analysis can follow the consequences of a code change farther than a reviewer can reasonably trace by hand. A reviewer may see that a value is checked before use in the usual path. An analyzer can follow that value across function boundaries and find an error path where the check never happens, even if no test exercises that path.

In a large codebase, the relevant facts may be spread across files, libraries, and teams. An analyzer applies the same checks across millions of lines and reruns them as the code changes. That makes it good at finding rare combinations of otherwise ordinary code, such as an early return that leaks a resource or an unexpected input that reaches a sensitive operation.

Analyzers can raise false alarms and miss bugs their rules don’t cover. Their advantage is the ability to check specific properties consistently at a scale that human review and testing alone struggle to match.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Even expert reviewers have limited attention. They tend to follow the paths a change is meant to affect, while a serious bug may live on a rarely used error path or in an assumption shared across several files. Tests can miss the same bug if they never exercise the triggering conditions.

Static analyzers apply the same checks across the codebase on every run. For example, an analyzer can trace a value from a function that sometimes returns null to a caller that dereferences it, even if no test has triggered the failure. The tool can flag that path, and engineers can use their knowledge of the system to judge whether it can occur in production.
